sources.summary: My friend John Varah, who has died aged 67 of heart failure, was one of Britain’s most influential community artists. A cultural anarchist dedicated to creating festivals, parades and illuminated spectacles, he was an inventor as much as an artist, surrounded by coils of wire, soldering irons and improbable contraptions as he coaxed ideas into life. Over the years he created and curated a number of popular events, including the annual Burning the Clocks ritual in Brighton, in which, on the winter solstice, thousands of people walk through the city carrying handmade paper-and-willow lanterns containing their hopes and dreams for the year. sources.summary: Laurence Lévesque’s powerful documentary follows a woman who discovers a support network among her mother’s generation of survivors of the nuclear blast No words are spoken during the first five minutes of Laurence Lévesque’s documentary. In a rustic house in the city of Nagasaki, a Japanese woman in her 60s, Noriko, draws back the curtains to let in the glow of dawn. The tranquil mood, however, is deceptive. Once her childhood home, the place holds a lifetime of secrets, which Norkia only discovers after her parents’ death. While clearing out the house, she comes across letters received by her mother that shed light on her turmoil as a survivor of Nagasaki’s atomic bombing in 1945. Noriko has always known her mother was a hibakusha – a term referring to people who survived the nuclear bombs. Already scarred by psychological and physical trauma, the victims also faced ostracism in the postwar period, with many barred from work or marriage. Perhaps due to the stigma, Noriko’s mother mentioned little of this to Noriko and her siblings. The letters, however, reveal a moving network of support among the hibakusha , as well as those who lost their loved ones in the bombings. In one heartbreaking note, a grieving mother speaks of sending a healthy son into the army, only to receive his hair and clipped nails in return. Continue reading...
sources.title: Okurimono review – a heartbreaking dispatch from survivors of the Nagasaki bomb

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: There are glimpses of Atkinson’s subtle brilliance in this gentle noirish mystery set around the Festival of Britain In 1951, in a desperate attempt to raise the spirits of a shattered nation, the government came up with the Festival of Britain, a celebration of national creativity, grit and ingenuity. It is a moment in history that could have been designed for Kate Atkinson, who loves nothing more than a quirky detail and a cast of British eccentrics. Harry Flynn (definitely think Errol), the quietly magnetic hero of Our Noble Selves, has survived Burma as a foreign correspondent turned war reporter. After a doomed marriage to a war widow called Ivy, and a stint in a mock-Tudor semi in Wealdstone with her, her eight-year-old daughter Veronica and a terrier, Mrs Betty, he resumes his bachelor life in London. A chance encounter with his old newspaper boss, Gerald Barry, leads him to a job compiling the festival’s poetry anthology. Barry provides a handy introduction: “The country’s stuck in the doldrums; we need to see the future,” he explains. The festival will celebrate “the Land and the People … Our love of country, love of freedom, love of nature, pride in craftsmanship, our reputation for tolerance and fair play.” Continue reading...

items.headline: 台南醫美手術致死案
